content: Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is a prevalent gynecological condition, accounting for approximately 20% of all gynecological referrals. The condition has a wide range of potential causes, many of which share overlapping symptoms, making its management particularly challenging for clinicians. The etiology of CPP is highly heterogeneous, and in many cases, a definitive diagnosis cannot be established. In such instances, the term chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS) is often applied. CPPS is defined as pelvic pain persisting for at least six months, which may include conditions like pelvic congestion syndrome but excludes pain caused by identifiable conditions such as endometriosis. Various surgical interventions have been employed, either alone or in combination with non-surgical treatments, to manage CPPS, but their outcomes have been inconsistent. Surgical procedures are inherently invasive and carry associated risks, necessitating a thorough evaluation of their effectiveness before they are widely adopted for managing CPPS. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of surgical interventions in women with CPPS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group Specialised Register of Controlled Trials, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, as of April 23, 2021. Additional sources, such as citation lists, trial registries, conference proceedings, and grey literature, were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women with CPPS, evaluating any surgical intervention. Outcome measures included pain scores, adverse events, psychological outcomes, quality of life (QoL), and the need for analgesia. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion and extracted data using Cochrane guidelines. Data on randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and reporting were collected. Results were pooled using mean differences (MDs) or odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and standardized mean differences (SMDs) were calculated for outcomes reported on different scales. The GRADE criteria were applied to evaluate the overall certainty of the evidence. Four studies, involving 216 women with CPP of unknown cause, met the inclusion criteria. The following findings were reported: 1. Adhesiolysis Compared to No Surgery or Diagnostic Laparoscopy: The effect of adhesiolysis on pelvic pain scores at three months postoperatively was uncertain (MD −7.3, 95% CI −29.9 to 15.3; low-certainty evidence). Similar uncertainty was noted at six months (MD −14.3, 95% CI −35.9 to 7.3; low-certainty evidence) and 12 months (MD 0.00, 95% CI −4.60 to 4.60; very low-certainty evidence). Adhesiolysis may improve emotional wellbeing (MD 24.90, 95% CI 7.92 to 41.88; low-certainty evidence) and social support (MD 23.90, 95% CI −1.77 to 49.57; low-certainty evidence) as measured by the Endometriosis Health Profile-30. It may also improve the emotional (MD 32.30, 95% CI 13.16 to 51.44; low-certainty evidence) and physical (MD 22.90, 95% CI 10.97 to 34.83; low-certainty evidence) components of the 12-item Short Form QoL tool compared to diagnostic laparoscopy. The safety of adhesiolysis remains uncertain due to low-certainty evidence and a lack of structured adverse event reporting. No studies reported on psychological outcomes or the need for analgesia. 2. Laparoscopic Uterosacral Ligament Ablation or Resection (LUNA) Compared to Diagnostic Laparoscopy or Other Treatments: The effect of LUNA on pelvic pain at three months postoperatively was uncertain (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.40 to 3.93; low-certainty evidence). Similar uncertainty was noted at six months (MD −2.10, 95% CI −4.38 to 0.18; very low-certainty evidence) and 12 months. One study (56 participants) found no significant difference in the effect of LUNA on non-cyclical pain (P = 0.854) or dyspareunia (P = 0.41). However, LUNA showed a benefit for dysmenorrhea (P = 0.045) and dyschezia (P = 0.05). The effect of LUNA compared to vaginal uterosacral ligament resection on pelvic pain at 12 months was uncertain (MD 2.00, 95% CI 0.47 to 3.53; very low-certainty evidence). The safety of LUNA or resection remains uncertain due to a lack of structured adverse event reporting. Women undergoing LUNA may require more postoperative analgesia than those receiving other treatments (P < 0.001; 1 study, 74 participants). No studies reported psychological outcomes or QoL. Conclusions: The current evidence does not provide certainty regarding the benefits of adhesiolysis or LUNA for managing pain in women with CPPS. Adhesiolysis may offer some QoL benefits, particularly in emotional wellbeing and social support, as measured by validated tools. However, the evidence on adverse events, especially long-term outcomes, is insufficient and poorly reported. Consequently, there is limited support for the routine use of these surgical interventions in the management of CPPS.
